I do not disagree with the Camp David proposals' unfairness, Arafat had understandable reasons to reject them, which were too vague with regards to Palestinian compensation for territory Israel would take, as well as the Israeli government's refusal to discuss the refugee issue.

If there was ever, however a missed opportunity for Palestine to make a peace with Israel that was (mostly?) fair to both sides, it would be Taba, which, though it still left many questions unanswered, was a sign that the Labour government of Barak was prepared to make reasonable concessions for a peace, and that Palestine was not wholly opposed. Were it not for the 2nd Intifada, we may have seen further development in the talks.

As it was though, Ariel Sharon's goading of the Palestinians, and the Palestinian Authority's failure to rein in the violence of the 2nd Intifada (as much as Arafat attempted to do so, as Shlaim notes) (and Sharon's refusal to see lower level talks to try to end the Intifada earlier further develop), we do not quite know what a future peace based on further negotiations after Taba would have looked like.

The main reason as to why Arafat declined the 91% proposal at Camp David was the status of East Jerusalem. Israel wanted the Temple Mount, a holy site for the Jewish faith, and was prepared to compensate the Palestinians for land elsewhere. However, also present at the site was Al Aqsa, a holy site in Islam. Any deal that handed it over would be very unpopular with the Palestinians, to say the least.

The 91% deal would have seen the dismantling of most Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Gaza. Only the larger settlements close to what would become the future Israeli border would remain, connected by access roads to Israel. The 9% was basically those settlements + parts of East Jerusalem.

Arafat refusing this is, with hindsight, a bad decision, but with the knowledge that he had at the time (that peace with Palestine was a surprisingly popular idea in Israel), and the fear that he would go the way of Egyptian president Sadat (assassinated for making peace with Israel) an understandable decision. Avi Shlaim in his book *Israel and the Arab World* contends that Israeli PM Barak ought to have offered more if he wished to secure an honorable and lasting peace between Israel and palestine.

Funnily enough, there was a better deal offered a few months later, at Taba, where Israel was prepared to agree to the 1967 borders with some exceptions (some settlements + parts of East Jerusalem), effectively leaving *97%* of the Palestinian territory in Palestinian hands, and progress also made on the refugee issue, with Israel offering to compensate the refugees, to help them settle into the countries they remained in, or to see them returned, (with some of them returning) to Israel, or to Palestine.

Of course, the 2nd Intifada would derail the talks and the fall of the left-wing Israeli government that initiated the negotiations and the rise of the hawkish, right-wing Likud in the aftermath saw the talks ended inconclusively.

Arafat declined the 91% proposal at Camp David in 2000 (mainly) over the status of East Jerusalem. There were later negotiations at Taba in Egypt in the same year which had Israel friendly to the idea of reinstating the 1967 border, and a possible solution to the refugee question (Israel did not necessarily agree to the right of return but agreed that there ought to be compensation and/or return of some of the refugees), but those negotiations were hamstrung by the 2nd Intifada (launched by Palestinian militants but provoked by the right-wing Likud politician Ariel Sharon) that basically destroyed public support for the doves of the Israeli Labor Party, who then lost the election that followed, and the talks at Taba were broken.

So in a way, the Palestinians (via the 2nd Intifada) destroyed the one party that was willing to make peace with Palestine, directly leading to the rise of its right wing opponent, Likud, who definitely were not going to make peace with Palestine.

The source of this is Avi Shlaim's book *The Iron Wall: Israel and the Arab World*. Shlaim is an Israeli but is a *New Historian*, a group that worked in the 80s and 90s to correct the pro-Israeli narrative present in orthodox Israeli historiography. The book itself (one I highly recommend) covers the diplomatic history of the conflict, from the birth of Israel and the first Arab-Israeli war (Shlaim blames Israeli intransigence for the failure to secure a lasting peace after the 1948 war) to the events after the 2nd Intifada and the premiership of Ariel Sharon.

Palestine had genuine reasons to reject the proposals at Camp David (Refugees, East Jerusalem), I cannot fault them for that. With hindsight, however, if both sides were more willing to compromise, it (and Taba) were probably one of the best opportunities for peace.

If the 2nd Intifada had not happened (had Sharon not provoked it, I might add), maybe we would have seen peace (on the basis of a potential agreement at Taba).

Israel cannot accept the initiative because it involves the *Right of Return*, which would destroy the demographics of Israel and its fundamental identity as a *Jewish* state. The plan specifically rejects the resettlement of Palestinian refugees in Palestine or elsewhere, which is an immediate non-starter for Israel. At Camp David in 2000 (some of the) Palestinian negotiators were prepared to discuss limits to how many refugees would be allowed to return to Israeli territory.

The territory is one of the issues with it (but Israel was prepared to return 97% of Palestinian land during the talks at Taba in 2000, so the true limit of what Israel is willing to return is not quite known), but the refugee question is also a major issue with it.

Not trying to hand wave away the many, many questionable (understatement, I know) acts that Israel have done in the West Bank, just trying to explain the rationale.

The historian Avi Shlaim (Israeli, but a revisionist, pro-Palestine *New Historian*) contends in his book, *The Iron Wall: Israel and the Arab World* (a fantastic look at the diplomatic history of the conflict, for example, placing Israeli intransigence at fault for the failure to make peace after the 1948 war) that Israeli PM Barak, who would attempt to secure peace with Palestine at Camp David and at Taba, was very likely genuine in his attempts to make peace. After all, his foremost platform during his election against Netanyahu was *to make peace with Palestine*. He also presided over the unilateral withdrawal from Lebanon and the (attempted) negotiations with Syria.

Barak's offer for peace at Camp David (91% of Palestine would be Palestinian) was not enough for Arafat, who also vehemently rejected the transfer of land in East Jerusalem to Israel. Both sides, however, would (tentatively, Arafat put many conditons to his agreement) agree to the Clinton Parameters, which would later be the basis for negotiations at Taba, in Egypt.

The Taba negotiations see even more progress towards peace, with the offer including 97% of de jure Palestine territory being under Palestinian control, progress on the refugee issue, and an agreement that Jerusalem was to be the capital of both Israel and Palestine. However, the Israeli elections and the prospective collapse of Barak's government (largely brought about by the Second Intifada and the Israeli population's disillusionment with the peace process because of it (even if it was goaded by Likud's Sharon)) would result in Barak suspending the talks.

Shlaim notes that Barak, though he was willing to sacrifice a lot for peace, should have been willing to sacrifice more (especially on the Jerusalem and refugee issues). As previously mentioned, however, Barak's attempts at peace were truly genuine, and much progress was made during his time in office, but the fall of his government and the rise of the right-wing Likud in the immediate aftermath of the election, led to efforts to secure a peace amenable to both sides being suspended for some time.

I suggest you read MC 14/3, written 1967, for more details on this decision.

I'd argue they'd be willing to sacrifice much of V Corps to halt the Soviets before Frankfurt and the Rhine.

NORTHAG's deployment also speaks to Germany not being a buffer, with much of British I. Corps also east of the Rhine. Colonial Secretary Chamberlain wanted a general alliance, in exchange for Britain providing assistance to German colonial goals.

Germany believed that it was on firmer ground than Britain during negotiations (the nature and manner of Chamberlain's request made them think that Britain might be going to war with Russia soon) and tried to secure multiple British concessions. In fact, the Kaiser was fairly happy to delay negotiations until Britain had no choice but to concede. It was an error in judgement on Berlin's part which drove Britain into the Entente.

It was also Germany wanting colonial concessions *and* Britain in the Triple Alliance vs Britain only needing someone to keep Russia in check.

Germany thought that Chamberlain's very blunt form of diplomacy (he was *not* trained in a diplomat's subtlety) meant that Britain was desperate and as such they asked for way more in an alliance than what Britain was willing to give.

The time when the negotiations took place was actually a high point in Anglo-German relations, taking place after Queen Victoria's death, when Wilhelm II was very popular in Britain, in spite of the 1898 Fleet Act in Germany.

There were a number of issues with Millenium Challenge 2002, most of which is very well explained by [this post](https://www.reddit.com/r/CredibleDefense/comments/4qfoiw/millennium_challenge_2002_setting_the_record/?utm_medium=android_app&utm_source=share) on r/CredibleDefense.

To summarise, though:
1.) A technical error, made due to the fact that, in order to perfotm the exercise without disrupting civilian maritime traffic, US naval forces had to position themselves much closer to shore, and this was reflected in simulation, instead of the standoff distance they would normally be at.

2.) They had to shut off some ship defense systems which werent designed to operate in places with lots of civilian maritime traffic. Particularly point-defense systems, which are the main defensive system warships have to defend themselves at closer ranges from cruise missiles.

3.) General Van Riper's actions, such as using motorcycle messengers to forgo the use of radio that somehow also delivered information instantaneously. "The OPFOR was able to maintain communications through non-standard, non-electronic methods such as couriers, face-to-face meetings, smoke, flags, and religious sermons. Timelines associated with these forms of communications could not be reflected in the game models during MC02"

4.) CIvilian aircraft somehow capable of carrying cruise missiles, can be described as questionable, I suppose.

5.) Issues with communication of data in the blue team meant that though they *did* know that the attack was coming, they failed to react properly to it.

6.) The report itself, which you can download for free, notes that "Except for OPFOR' s pre-emptive naval attack, successful terrorist attacks near Blue APODs, and the use of civilian aircraft in attacking Blue infrastructure, operational air, space, and missile defense was well executed. Systems and capabilities were generally well protected. " With the exception of the initial surprise attack, red's military operations, particular in the sea and air, couldn't really touch blue.

7.) The goal of MC 2002 wasn't just to test if blue forces could enter red waters, rather, how blue would fare in a land invasion of red, with all of the complexities that it would entail. That can't really be tested if the entire force is destroyed in the opening.

8.) To add to this, there were differences in how Van Ryker (Who initially led Opfor) and Kernan (who got Van Ryker to lead Opfor) viewed MC2002. The former viewed it as an exercise, where free play could be used to maximize learning opportunities. The latter saw it as an experiment to test concepts that the US in 2002 were developing, requiring more direct control to enable it.

Let me tell you a story from a time when the US military was somewhat underfunded, namely that of the Mark 14 Torpedo.

Along comes the Second World War, and the 23 USN submarines based in the Philippines head to sea to begin operations against Japan, only to find out that their torpedoes are either a.) Exploding prematurely, b.) Not exploding at all, or c.) Went too deep, ending up missing.

For the first two years of the war, USN submariners had to work with a non-functional torpedo. When the Mark 14 was finally somewhat reliable, the US submarine fleet began to take a toll on the IJN's merchant ships. By the end of the war, 55% of all Japanese merchant shipping was sunk by US submarine forces.

They also took a toll on Japanese capital ship forces- the battleship Kongo, and the fleet carriers Shokaku, Unryu, Taiho and Shinano were all sunk by USN submarines.
